prompt:
# A naming decision keeps getting reopened and never lands

You are a product manager. The customer-facing name for a new fast-turnaround
risk score at your company has been reopened at least three times over the life
of the product, and no name has survived past the review cycle in which it was
chosen.

Round one settled on language describing the score as an early estimate;
reviewers later objected that this made the score sound experimental without
explaining why the number differed from the fully-processed version. Round two
tried distinguishing an estimated score from a final one; a senior design
reviewer objected that this fragmented terminology already used consistently
elsewhere in the product family. Round three tried distinguishing the score by
its underlying processing method; this was immediately re-litigated because
every version of the score technically qualified under that same description.

You are now heading into a fourth round. Every prior round had customer research
showing a different way the current candidate name confused people, and no
candidate has ever been unambiguously better than the alternatives it replaced.
The underlying API field name was locked early on for backward-compatibility
reasons and can no longer change regardless of what customer-facing name is
chosen. The naming also needs to stay consistent across a family of related
products, which adds reviewers and constraints beyond just this one team.

How do you approach this fourth round, and why?

Constraints:
- The underlying API field name is already locked and cannot change.
- The naming must stay consistent across a family of related products.
- Three previous rounds have each been overturned in the following review cycle.
response:
## What I'd conclude before doing anything

Three rounds, three different names, three different objections, and no candidate ever clearly better than what it replaced. That pattern tells me the problem isn't that we haven't found the right word yet. It's that we've been running an optimization against a moving target: each round fixes the previous round's complaint and gets rejected on a new axis nobody had stated up front. If I run round four the same way — generate candidates, test them, pick one, send it to review — I should expect the same result, because nothing about the process has changed.

So I'd treat round four primarily as a process decision, and only secondarily as a naming decision.

## What I'd actually do

**1. Get the criteria agreed before any names are on the table.**
I'd go to the reviewers — including the design reviewer with the product-family concern — and get written agreement on what the name has to do and, critically, what it's allowed to sacrifice. The three prior objections give me the axes: (a) shouldn't sound experimental or unreliable, (b) must fit existing product-family terminology, (c) must actually distinguish this score from the fully-processed one. I'd force a ranking. Something like: family consistency is a hard constraint, distinguishability is required, "sounds provisional" is acceptable if the adjacent copy explains why. The point is that a reviewer who signs the criteria can't later reject a name for a reason that isn't in them.

**2. Stop asking the name to do the whole job.**
The round-one objection — "makes it sound experimental *without explaining why* it differs" — is a documentation complaint dressed as a naming complaint. No two-word label is going to explain that this score is computed before all inputs have landed. I'd propose the name plus a fixed one-line descriptor that travels with it everywhere it appears (UI, docs, marketing). This removes a whole class of objections from the name itself and gives the customer research something realistic to test.

**3. Choose from the existing candidates rather than inventing a fourth.**
We already have three names with known failure modes and customer research on each. A fresh candidate would just have an *unknown* failure mode, which will be discovered in the next review cycle and look worse by comparison. I'd put the prior three (plus possibly the raw API field name, since developers will see it anyway and alignment has real value) into a single comparative study with one protocol, and pick the one that confuses least — not the one that confuses nobody, because that one doesn't exist. Prior research was "does this name confuse people?", which always returns yes. I need "which of these do people interpret correctly most often?"

**4. Make the decision closable.**
Named owner (me, or whoever the family-level authority is — I'd find out and make it explicit), a time box, the reviewers who signed the criteria, and a decision record stating the tradeoffs accepted. Then a reopening rule: after the deadline, an objection has to show the chosen name is *worse on the agreed criteria* than a specific alternative, not merely that it has a flaw. Everything has a flaw; we've already proven that empirically.

## Why this rather than trying harder on the name

The cost of continued churn is real and mostly invisible: docs, SDKs, marketing, and partner teams are all waiting or writing around the gap, and every reversal erodes confidence in the next decision. Against that, the marginal difference between the least-bad name and the actual-best name is probably small — the research already suggests the candidates are roughly equivalent, each just failing differently. Given the product-family constraint, changing later is genuinely expensive, which is exactly why I want the decision to be made once with the constraints visible, rather than made a fourth time with the same blind spots.

What I'd want to know before I start: what the locked API field name actually is (if it's usable, that's a strong tiebreaker), whether the score has shipped to any customers under any of the prior names, and who has the authority to close a decision at the family level rather than just the team level. If that last person doesn't exist, finding or creating them is the real work of round four.
